questions.question_text:
**[Precision Pump Manufacturing Firm Case]**
A mid-sized engineering company manufactures industrial pumps for chemical plants, food processors, and water-treatment facilities. The company offers 45 pump models with multiple motor sizes and casing materials (cast iron, stainless steel, polymer-lined). Most customer orders are configured after order receipt.
The factory has machining, casting finishing, heat treatment, painting, and final assembly departments. Machines are arranged by function. Shafts, impellers, housings, and brackets are produced internally, while bearings, seals, and motors are purchased from suppliers.
Because demand fluctuates and each order has different specifications, jobs wait between departments. Final assembly combines purchased and manufactured parts, then each pump is pressure-tested before shipping.
Based on this description, answer the following questions.
questions.explanation: Shared passage for the questions that follow.

questions.question_text: Which production system best describes this factory?
questions.explanation: A jumbled flow system is characterized by high variety, low-to-medium volume, and customized or configured-to-order production where jobs follow non-standard, jumbled routings across functional departments.

questions.question_text: Which layout is most likely used?
questions.explanation: In a process layout (functional layout), machines and workstations performing similar functions (such as machining, heat treatment, painting) are grouped together to handle high variety and customized workflows.

questions.question_text: Where is the highest inventory likely concentrated?
questions.explanation: Because products are configured after order receipt and jobs wait between functional departments due to varying processing specifications, inventory builds up heavily as raw materials and work-in-process (WIP).

questions.question_text: Which action would most improve delivery speed without harming variety?

options.C: Increase finished-goods stock of all variants

questions.explanation: Reducing machine setup times enables smaller batch sizes and rapid changeovers between diverse pump models, significantly cutting manufacturing lead times while fully preserving product variety.

questions.question_text:
**[Project Network Analysis]**
Please consider the below data on project network problem to answer the next set of questions.

| Activity | Predecessor | Normal Duration (weeks) |
| :---: | :---: | :---: |
| A | - | 3 |
| B | - | 4 |
| C | A | 2 |
| D | B | 5 |
| E | C | 4 |
| F | D | 3 |
| G | C | 6 |
| H | E | 2 |
| I | E, F | 5 |
| J | G, H, I | 3 |
questions.explanation: Shared passage for the questions that follow.

questions.question_text: Which activity is a merge point?
questions.explanation: A merge point in a project network is an activity that has multiple immediate predecessors. Activity I requires both activities E and F to be completed before it can start.

questions.question_text: If activity D is completed early, which activity can begin earlier immediately?
questions.explanation: Activity D is the sole immediate predecessor of activity F. Therefore, completing activity D early allows activity F to begin immediately earlier.

questions.question_text: If the manager can crash only one activity to reduce total project completion time most effectively, which activity is the best candidate?
questions.explanation: Activity J lies on the critical path (B → D → F → I → J, duration 20 weeks) and is the final converging activity through which all parallel paths pass. Crashing J directly reduces overall project duration without being constrained by parallel paths.

questions.question_text: Which activity is the final merge point, just before project completion?
questions.explanation: Activity J has predecessors G, H, and I converging into it, making it the final merge point in the network prior to project completion.

questions.question_text: If activity C is delayed by 2 weeks, which activities are directly affected first?
questions.explanation: Activities E and G both have activity C as their immediate predecessor. Consequently, any delay in activity C directly impacts the start of activities E and G first.

questions.question_text: Which of the following activities has no predecessor?
questions.explanation: Both activities A and B have no predecessors (denoted by `-`), allowing them to start immediately at the beginning of the project.

questions.question_text: If activity F finishes early, what is the earliest likely benefit?
questions.explanation: Activity F is an immediate predecessor to activity I. If F finishes early, activity I may start earlier, provided its other predecessor (activity E) is also complete.

questions.question_text: Which sequence represents a valid path in the network?
questions.explanation: Tracing immediate predecessors: A has no predecessor, C follows A, E follows C, I follows E, and J follows I. Thus, A → C → E → I → J forms a technologically valid sequence through the network.

questions.question_text: A c-chart is used to monitor:

options.B: Number of defects per inspection unit

questions.explanation: A c-chart is an attribute control chart based on the Poisson distribution used to monitor the count (number) of defects per constant unit of inspection.

questions.question_text:
In a service organization, the following decisions are taken:
• D1: Cross-training employees across departments
• D2: Installing self-service kiosks
What is the most likely impact?

options.A: D1 increases cost; D2 reduces flexibility
options.B: D1 increases flexibility; D2 increases speed
options.C: D1 reduces quality; D2 reduces speed
options.D: D1 decreases utilization; D2 decreases quality

questions.explanation: Cross-training employees (D1) increases workforce flexibility by allowing personnel to shift dynamically across departments, while self-service kiosks (D2) automate routine tasks to increase delivery speed.

questions.question_text: A station has two parallel machines, each producing 12 units/hour. It is followed by another station with capacity 18 units/hour. What is the overall process capacity?
questions.explanation:
1. The first station has two parallel machines, yielding a combined capacity of $12 + 12 = 24\text{ units/hour}$.
2. The second station has a capacity of $18\text{ units/hour}$.
3. The overall process capacity is governed by the bottleneck: $\min(24, 18) = 18\text{ units/hour}$.

questions.question_text: Little’s Law states that:
questions.explanation: Little's Law is a fundamental relationship in operations stating that average Work-in-Process (WIP) equals average Throughput rate multiplied by average Flow Time ($L = \lambda W$).

questions.question_text: If average WIP inventory is 40 units and average flow rate is 8 units/hour, what is the average lead time?
questions.explanation:
Using Little's Law:
$$\text{Lead Time} = \frac{\text{WIP}}{\text{Flow Rate}} = \frac{40\text{ units}}{8\text{ units/hour}} = 5\text{ hours}.$$

questions.question_text: The process capability index (Cpk) is primarily used to assess:

options.D: Process centering and spread relative to specs

questions.explanation: $C_{pk}$ measures how well a process satisfies customer specifications by taking into account both the overall process spread ($6\sigma$) and the centering of the process mean relative to the specification limits.

questions.question_text: Which statement is correct about process capability index (Cpk)?

options.A: Higher Cpk indicates process is closer to target and within specs
options.C: Lower Cpk means process is faster

questions.explanation: A higher $C_{pk}$ demonstrates that the process distribution has minimal variation and is well-centered within customer specification limits, leading to fewer defects.

questions.question_text: A bakery uses flour at a constant rate of 80 kg per day throughout the year. Its regular supplier, S1, charges ₹20 per kg. The annual holding cost is ₹4 per kg. For Supplier S1, there is no order-processing charge. However, the bakery must arrange transportation separately, which costs ₹144 per order/trip. The lead time from S1 is 4 days. A new supplier, S2, has recently started operations. S2 charges ₹19 per kg and provides free delivery. However, placing each order with S2 requires staff time worth ₹100 per order. The lead time from S2 is 7 days. Assume 365 days per year, constant demand, and no shortages.
questions.explanation: Shared passage for the questions that follow.

questions.question_text: Compared with Supplier S1, Supplier S2 is:
questions.explanation: Supplier S2 offers a lower unit price (₹19/kg compared to S1's ₹20/kg) but has a longer delivery lead time (7 days compared to S1's 4 days).

questions.question_text: What is annual demand for flour?
questions.explanation:
1. Daily demand $d = 80\text{ kg/day}$.
2. Number of days per year $= 365$.
$$\text{Annual Demand } (D) = 80 \times 365 = 29,200\text{ kg}.$$

questions.question_text: What is economic ordering quantity (EOQ) from Supplier S1?
questions.explanation:
For Supplier S1, $D = 29,200\text{ kg}$, $S = ₹144$, and $H = ₹4/\text{kg/year}$:
$$\text{EOQ} = \sqrt{\frac{2DS}{H}} = \sqrt{\frac{2 \times 29,200 \times 144}{4}} = \sqrt{2,102,400} \approx 1,450\text{ kg}.$$

questions.question_text: If bakery buys from Supplier S2 at EOQ, average inventory is:
questions.explanation:
1. For Supplier S2, $D = 29,200\text{ kg}$, $S = ₹100$, and $H = ₹4/\text{kg/year}$:
$$\text{EOQ}_{S2} = \sqrt{\frac{2 \times 29,200 \times 100}{4}} = \sqrt{1,460,000} \approx 1,208.3\text{ kg}.$$
2. Average cycle inventory is:
$$\frac{\text{EOQ}}{2} = \frac{1,208.3}{2} \approx 604.15\text{ kg} \approx 604\text{ kg}.$$

questions.question_text: Which supplier has higher reorder point, and why?

options.B: S2, because lead time is longer
options.D: S1, because order size is larger

questions.explanation: Reorder point is given by $\text{ROP} = d \times L$. With daily consumption $d$ identical for both, Supplier S2 has a higher reorder point ($80 \times 7 = 560\text{ kg}$) than S1 ($80 \times 4 = 320\text{ kg}$) due to its longer lead time.

questions.question_text:
A manufacturing process is being monitored using a p-chart to track the proportion of defective units. Twenty samples are collected over regular intervals, each sample containing 90 units. The number of defectives observed in each sample is shown below:

| Sample | Number of Defectives | Sample | Number of Defectives |
| :---: | :---: | :---: | :---: |
| 1 | 8 | 11 | 9 |
| 2 | 10 | 12 | 13 |
| 3 | 6 | 13 | 11 |
| 4 | 14 | 14 | 12 |
| 5 | 7 | 15 | 8 |
| 6 | 12 | 16 | 7 |
| 7 | 11 | 17 | 10 |
| 8 | 9 | 18 | 14 |
| 9 | 13 | 19 | 11 |
| 10 | 8 | 20 | 9 |

The total number of defectives across all samples is 206. Since each sample contains 90 units, the average proportion defective across all samples is 0.1144. Based on this value, the Upper Control Limit (UCL) is 0.200 and the Lower Control Limit (LCL) is 0.027.

Based on Sample 20 and the given control limits, what conclusion can be drawn?

options.A: The point corresponding to Sample 20 lies above the Upper Control Limit (UCL).
options.B: The point corresponding to Sample 20 lies within the control limits.
options.C: The point corresponding to Sample 20 lies below the Lower Control Limit (LCL).

questions.explanation: For Sample 20, defectives = 9 out of $n = 90$, giving sample proportion $p_{20} = \frac{9}{90} = 0.10$. Since $0.027 < 0.10 < 0.200$, the sample point falls comfortably within the control limits.
